final_recommendation: The room converged on a trilateral package (65% probability) by late September 2018, structured around key trade-offs: U.S. drops Chapter 19 elimination, Canada opens 3-5% dairy access, hard sunset replaced by review mechanism, and facility-level labor enforcement designed for Democratic Congressional support.
minority_objections: 25% probability scenario: Canada refuses simultaneous dairy concessions AND Chapter 19 elimination, talks stall into 2019
10% probability scenario: Canada walks, U.S. proceeds with Mexico-only bilateral despite supply-chain disruption risks
AFL-CIO historically skeptical, needs convincing on labor enforcement teeth
Some auto parts suppliers may not comply with 75% RVC, shift sourcing to Asia
key_conflicts: Chapter 19 binational panels: USTR objective to eliminate vs. Canada's declared red line and parliamentary consensus
Canadian dairy access: U.S. domestic pressure (Wisconsin, New York) vs. Quebec/Ontario political toxicity for Trudeau
Sunset clause: U.S. leverage demand vs. auto industry investment certainty needs
Labor enforcement: facility-level mechanism seen as necessary by U.S. labor vs. sovereignty intrusion by Mexico
Dairy sweet spot extremely narrow: >5% triggers Canadian parliamentary revolt, <3% insufficient for U.S. dairy lobby
key_concessions: U.S. drops Chapter 19 elimination demand (lowest priority, highest Canadian resistance)
U.S. accepts review mechanism instead of hard sunset (can claim leverage preservation)
Canada opens 3-5% dairy market access via new TRQs (painful but survivable, framed as managed opening)
Canada accepts U.S.-Mexico auto rules with limited leverage after bilateral
Mexico accepts facility-level labor enforcement if procedurally defined and respects Mexican institutions
All parties accept 16-year term with 6-year review cycles instead of hard 5-year sunset
red_lines: Canada: Chapter 19 elimination = non-starter with parliamentary consensus
Canada: Full dismantlement of supply management = government collapse risk
Canada: Hard sunset clause = unacceptable investment uncertainty
U.S. labor (AFL-CIO, UAW): No paper commitments, enforcement must have teeth with facility-level rapid response
Auto industry: Hard 5-year sunset = immediate disinvestment trigger
U.S. dairy: Must show meaningful access (3%+ or politically insufficient)
Mexico: Labor reform acceptable only if enforcement respects Mexican institutions, no unilateral U.S. veto
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: AMLO transition risk (Dec 1, 2018): new administration may want to renegotiate despite pressure to close before transition
Canadian federal election timing (2019): deal becomes political football during campaign
Democratic House flip (November 2018 midterms): new majority changes Congressional dynamics for spring 2019 vote
Perverse outcome: some parts suppliers shift sourcing to Asia rather than comply with 75% RVC
Enforcement mechanisms untested: credibility questions during 2019-2020 implementation phase
Canadian Conservative government possibility (Oct 2019 election): potential renegotiation demands
downstream_risk_variables: Canadian dairy concessions political survivability: narrow window between <3% (U.S. insufficient) and >5% (Canadian revolt)
Mexican labor reform legislation passage and credibility: prerequisite for U.S. Democratic support
AFL-CIO position on labor enforcement design: determines Democratic Congressional votes
Auto industry phase-in timeline adequacy: 3-5 years needed to avoid production shutdowns
Congressional vote timing: sign by Dec 2018 → vote March-May 2019 in new Democratic House
Quebec/Ontario provincial premier positions on dairy: potential political crisis for Trudeau
Business community assessment of sunset/review mechanism clarity: determines lobbying position
uncertainty_notes: Three critical unresolved questions: (1) Can Canada politically survive 3-5% dairy opening with Quebec/Ontario management? (2) Will Democrats accept labor enforcement design or demand strengthening? (3) Does Mexico pass enabling labor legislation credibly before and after AMLO transition? Timing cascade: need trilateral announcement by end September 2018, signing before Dec 1 Mexican transition, Congressional vote spring 2019 in new Democratic House.

marker_evidence.auto_rules_bottleneck: 75% RVC with labor-value-content locked via U.S.-Mexico bilateral, identified as Tier 2 significant bottleneck requiring 3-5 year phase-in, drove specific tiered phase-in proposal for existing vs. new models
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_key: Facility-level enforcement mechanism THE critical issue for Democratic Congressional votes, AFL-CIO support needed, drove specific rapid-response mechanism design with Mexican judicial role preserved
marker_evidence.canada_dairy_final_issue: Tier 1 decisive bottleneck, zero-sum quantifiable issue, sweet spot extremely narrow (3-5%), too much triggers parliamentary revolt, too little loses U.S. dairy lobby, drove specific TRQ structure and compensation package proposal
marker_evidence.dispute_settlement_canada_redline: Tier 1 decisive bottleneck, direct collision between USTR elimination objective and Canada's hardest red line with parliamentary consensus, drove U.S. concession to drop elimination demand in exchange for dairy access
marker_evidence.sunset_to_review_compromise: Tier 1 decisive bottleneck, hard sunset triggers immediate disinvestment, drove specific 16-year term with 6-year review cycles compromise to split difference between U.S. leverage and business certainty
marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Extensive analysis of all three countries' ratification fault lines shaped package design: labor enforcement for Democratic votes, dairy levels for Canadian survival, Mexican legislation timing, drove Congressional vote timing strategy
marker_evidence.supply_chain_adjustment: Raised as concern requiring 3-5 year phase-in and tiered staging, noted risk of perverse Asia sourcing shift, but did not block the 75% RVC agreement or change core auto rules outcome
marker_evidence.us_mexico_first_pressures_canada: U.S.-Mexico bilateral created take-it-or-leave-it artificial deadline pressure on Canada, drove Canada's limited negotiating leverage and acceptance of auto rules, explicit framing of trilateral formation strategy
